claims.statement: The model's visible tool set is assembled from layered sources — built-in middleware tools (filesystem, todo, subagent/task), caller-supplied tools=, backend capability gating, and profile excluded_tools — rather than a single hand-maintained list.

Tool visibility and permission are orthogonal: a tool advertised to and chosen by the model can still be denied, interrupted for human approval, or rejected at the tool-call boundary, so an offered tool is not necessarily an executable one.

_ToolExclusionMiddleware removes a profile's excluded tools from the model request in wrap_model_call and also rejects any call naming an excluded tool at the tool-call boundary with an 'is not available' error ToolMessage, because the executor still has the tool registered and dispatches on the emitted name.

_ToolExclusionMiddleware is wired into the graph only when the resolved profile has non-empty excluded_tools, and is appended after custom middleware so excluded tool names are stripped last and cannot be restored by a custom wrap_model_call.
Description overrides are applied to caller tools without mutating caller-owned objects: dict tools and BaseTool instances are copied and rewritten, while plain callables are returned unchanged.

The tool catalog for `dcode tools list` and the `/tools` command is derived by compiling the agent with an offline placeholder chat model (no credentials or network) and reading the bound tool node, so displayed tool names and descriptions cannot drift from what the model actually sees.

Because FilesystemMiddleware omits disallowed filesystem tools from the bound node entirely, the catalog forwards the allowlist to narrow enumeration and keeps a defensive backstop that logs loudly and returns the unfiltered list if a disallowed filesystem tool leaks through, rather than scrubbing the evidence that enforcement failed.
The built-in filesystem tool names are fixed by the FsToolName literal: ls, read_file, write_file, edit_file, delete, glob, grep, and execute.
read_file is mandatory in any filesystem allowlist: passing a tools= list that omits read_file raises ValueError.

When tools= is a list, FilesystemMiddleware omits disallowed tools entirely (never instantiating their factories) rather than merely hiding their schema, so a tool outside the allowlist never reaches the dispatchable tool node; tools='all' or the unset default enables every name subject to backend capability.

execute is a backend-gated tool available only when the resolved backend implements SandboxBackendProtocol (a shell); when execution is unsupported the tool is filtered from the request at model-call time and, if reached, returns an execution-not-available error.

At request time FilesystemMiddleware filters capability-gated execute and delete tools the backend cannot serve, reconciles grep and execute descriptions to active tools, and appends the virtual-vs-host path routing prompt when execute is active.

grep searches for a literal (non-regex) pattern, with a total match cap governed by grep_max_count (default 1000, overridable per call via max_count or disabled with None), and its description points at the execute tool with rg for genuine regex only when execute is active.

Oversized tool results are evicted to the filesystem under the artifacts root, except for tools that truncate their own output or return minimal confirmations (ls, glob, grep, read_file, edit_file, write_file, delete), which are excluded from eviction.

FilesystemPermission rules are enforced inside the tool implementations (not by removing tools) via _check_fs_permission, which matches operation and path against wcmatch globs and returns allow, deny, or interrupt.

Permission enforcement distinguishes exact-path tools (read_file, write_file, edit_file) that fire on their single path from bulk tools (ls, glob, grep, delete) that fire when their search subtree could overlap an anchored rule prefix, and a pathless bulk call such as grep(path=None) fires unconditionally for any interrupt-mode rule.

FilesystemPermission path patterns are validated at construction (must start with '/', must not contain '..' or '~'), and permissions are rejected when combined with execution-capable backends unless every rule path is scoped to routes, because tool-level permissions for execute are not implemented.

dcode resolves extension tool ownership before calling create_deep_agent: it removes supplied tools whose name is registered by an extension, adds extension tool units, similarly replaces colliding middleware, and installs the extension runtime middleware.
dcode adapts each MCP tool through langchain.mcp.as_langchain_tool, requires an asynchronous StructuredTool, normalizes its arguments, and records MCP server and original-name provenance in metadata.

dcode produces provider-safe MCP names by sanitizing server and tool names and limiting them to 64 characters; changed or overlong names receive a deterministic SHA-256-derived suffix, and a deterministic second pass resolves exported-name collisions.

MCP discovery preflights and connects servers concurrently with a bound, but returns server information in configuration order and the combined tool list sorted by name; unavailable servers are represented with status information rather than contributing tools.

Backend ReadResult validates pagination metadata at construction so paired window fields, forward bounds, total length, and the next offset remain consistent; the filesystem middleware, not a backend, applies line-number formatting.

The backend protocol treats grep and glob truncation as partial valid results rather than hard failures, and its asynchronous grep wrapper enforces both a wait timeout and the requested total match cap even when a concrete backend lacks max_count support.

LocalShellBackend provides shell capability by running commands directly on the host through subprocess with shell=True; virtual_mode affects filesystem path mapping but does not restrict those commands, so it is not a sandbox or a filesystem security boundary.

Filesystem integration tests verify that parallel writes merge StateBackend file updates and that invalid paths become ToolMessage errors, while concurrent edits of the same file are deliberately marked xfail because reducers and backends can race.
validate_path normalizes virtual filesystem paths and rejects traversal, leading-home, and Windows-drive forms, but it is not a shell-execution restriction.

The shared backend glob matcher gives glob and grep include globs the same path semantics: basename matching at any depth without a slash, search-root-relative matching with a slash, explicit dotfile matching, and central rejection of traversal segments.

MCPToolMiddleware normalizes marked MCP-tool arguments and converts recognized stale-token failures into actionable error ToolMessages, while preserving server ToolException handling and propagating unrelated exceptions.

MCP server status records an explicit consistency invariant: ok has tools and no error, while a non-ok server has an error and no tools; disabled and authentication failures are therefore visible operational states rather than silent absence.
